questions.stem: Which form completes 'Wenn ich mehr Zeit ___, würde ich ein Instrument lernen.'?
questions.explanation: An imagined condition needs the subjunctive II, and for 'haben' with 'ich' that is 'hätte'. 'Hatte' is the ordinary imperfect ('I had'), and 'hätten' is the plural form.

questions.stem: What is the subjunctive II of 'sein' for 'wir'?
questions.explanation: The subjunctive II of 'sein' adds an umlaut to the imperfect: 'wir waren' becomes 'wir wären' ('we would be'). 'Wärt' goes with 'ihr', and 'waren' is the plain past.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'If it were warmer, we could swim in the lake'?
options: 'Wenn es wärmer ist, konnten wir im See schwimmen.'
'Wenn es wärmer war, konnten wir im See schwimmen.'
'Wenn es wärmer wird, konnten wir im See schwimmen.'
'Wenn es wärmer wäre, könnten wir im See schwimmen.'
questions.explanation: An unreal condition takes the subjunctive II in both halves: 'wäre' and 'könnten'. 'Wenn es wärmer war, konnten wir ...' is real past ('whenever it was warmer, we could').

questions.stem: Which sentence has the correct word order?
options: 'Wenn ich Geld hätte, ich würde ein Auto kaufen.'
'Wenn ich hätte Geld, würde ich ein Auto kaufen.'
'Wenn hätte ich Geld, würde ich ein Auto kaufen.'
'Wenn ich Geld hätte, würde ich ein Auto kaufen.'
questions.explanation: 'Wenn' sends its verb to the end of its clause, and the whole 'wenn' clause counts as the first element, so the main clause starts with its verb: 'hätte, würde ich'. Putting 'ich' straight after the comma breaks the verb-second rule.

questions.stem: In the polite request '___ Sie mir bitte sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?', which word fills the gap?
questions.explanation: 'Könnten Sie ...?' is the polite subjunctive of 'können' for 'Sie'. 'Konnten' is the imperfect ('were you able'), 'könntest' goes with 'du', and 'müssten' would ask whether the person would have to tell you.

questions.stem: Which is the most polite way to ask whether you may open the window?
questions.explanation: 'Dürfte ich ...?' is the subjunctive II of 'dürfen' and softens the request even more than 'Darf ich ...?'. The other sentences announce a decision, state a wish bluntly or give an order.

questions.stem: What does 'Eigentlich müsste ich heute Abend noch lernen' mean?
options: Really, I had to study this evening
Really, I must not study this evening
Really, I wanted to study this evening
Really, I ought to study this evening
questions.explanation: 'Müsste' is the subjunctive II of 'müssen' and means 'ought to' or 'should really'. The imperfect would be 'musste' ('had to'), with no umlaut.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'I would gladly help you'?
questions.explanation: 'Würde' plus a plain infinitive at the end is the conditional for most verbs. 'Wurde' without the umlaut is the imperfect of 'werden', and the infinitive after 'würde' takes no 'zu' and is not a participle.

questions.stem: 'Wenn ich du wäre, würde ich das Angebot annehmen.' What is the speaker doing?
options: Reporting what the speaker did with a past offer
Stating a firm plan to accept the offer tomorrow
Describing a condition that is likely to come true
Giving advice by imagining being in the other person's place
questions.explanation: 'Wenn ich du wäre' ('if I were you') is an unreal condition, so the speaker is advising, not describing fact. A likely, real condition would use the indicative, as in 'Wenn das Angebot kommt, nehme ich es an.'

questions.stem: Which sentence describes a real possibility rather than an imagined situation?
options: 'Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich mitkommen.'
'Wenn sie hier wäre, könnte sie uns helfen.'
'Wenn wir reich wären, würden wir reisen.'
'Wenn es morgen regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.'
questions.explanation: Rain tomorrow may really happen, so the indicative 'regnet ... bleiben' is used. The other three use the subjunctive II ('hätte', 'wäre', 'wären') because the speaker does not have time, she is not here and they are not rich.

questions.stem: What is the difference between 'Ich freue mich auf das Konzert' and 'Ich freue mich über das Konzert'?
options: The first looks forward to it; the second is pleased about it
The first is pleased about it; the second looks forward to it
The first is formal German; the second is only used in speech
The first is about one concert; the second about a concert series
questions.explanation: 'Sich freuen auf' means to look forward to something still to come. 'Sich freuen über' means to be pleased about something that has happened or is already there.

questions.stem: Which words complete 'Er entschuldigt sich ___ Trainer ___ seine Verspätung.'?
questions.explanation: You apologise to someone with 'sich entschuldigen bei' (here 'beim' = bei dem) and for something with 'für'. 'Zum' would mean going to the coach, and 'mit dem' is 'with', not 'to'.

questions.stem: Which preposition completes 'Wir warten schon seit einer Stunde ___ den Bus.'?
questions.explanation: German says 'warten auf' + accusative. 'Für' is the trap from English 'wait for'; 'warten für' is wrong.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Hast du Angst vor ___ Prüfung?'?
questions.explanation: 'Angst haben vor' takes the dative, and 'Prüfung' is feminine, so the article is 'der'. 'Die' would be accusative, which 'vor' only takes with movement.

questions.stem: In '___ habt ihr euch beschwert?' ('What did you complain about?'), which word fills the gap?
questions.explanation: The verb is 'sich beschweren über', so the question word is 'wo(r)' + 'über'. Each wo-compound copies the verb's own preposition; 'wofür' would ask what you were for.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Ich kümmere mich ___, dass alle eine Einladung bekommen.'?
questions.explanation: The verb is 'sich kümmern um', so the da-compound pointing to the 'dass' clause is 'darum'. 'Dafür' would suit 'sorgen für', a different verb.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Ich danke ___ für Ihre Hilfe.'?
questions.explanation: 'Danken' takes the dative, and the formal 'you' in the dative is 'Ihnen'. 'Sie' is the accusative form, the usual slip with this verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'My parents didn't like the film'?
options: 'Der Film hat meinen Eltern nicht gefallen.'
'Meine Eltern haben den Film nicht gefallen.'
'Der Film hat meine Eltern nicht gefallen.'
'Meinen Eltern hat den Film nicht gefallen.'
questions.explanation: With 'gefallen' the thing liked is the subject (der Film) and the person is in the dative (meinen Eltern). Making the parents the subject copies English 'like'.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Kannst du ___ Freund beim Umzug helfen?' ('your friend')?
questions.explanation: 'Helfen' takes the dative, and 'Freund' is masculine, so the possessive is 'deinem'. 'Deinen' would be accusative, as after a verb like 'besuchen'.

questions.stem: Which verb takes a dative object?
questions.explanation: 'Helfen' takes the dative: 'Ich helfe dir.' 'Fragen' looks as if it should, but it takes the accusative: 'Ich frage dich.'

questions.stem: Which words complete 'Mein Bruder hat mich überredet, mit ihm ins Konzert ___.'?
questions.explanation: After 'überreden' the infinitive clause needs 'zu' before the infinitive at the end: 'zu gehen'. A participle cannot follow 'zu'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: 'Wir hoffen, am Samstag schwimmen zu gehen zu.'
questions.explanation: A verb of motion such as 'gehen' takes a plain infinitive with no 'zu'. Verbs like 'vorhaben' and 'hoffen' need one 'zu': 'Wir haben vor, ... schwimmen zu gehen.'

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'She is saving to buy a car'?
options: 'Sie spart, um ein Auto zu kaufen.'
'Sie spart, für ein Auto zu kaufen.'
'Sie spart, um zu ein Auto kaufen.'
questions.explanation: Purpose is 'um ... zu', with 'um' opening the clause and 'zu' plus the infinitive at the end. 'Für' cannot introduce an infinitive clause.

questions.stem: In 'Um fit zu bleiben, geht sie dreimal pro Woche joggen', why does 'geht' come straight after the comma?
options: An um ... zu clause always sends the next verb to the end
'Geht' is an imperative, which always comes first
'Joggen' is separable, so 'geht' must move forward
The um ... zu clause is the first element, so the verb comes second
questions.explanation: A fronted clause fills the first position of the sentence, so the main verb follows it at once. The same happens after a 'wenn' clause.

questions.stem: What does 'Der Rasen wird jeden Samstag gemäht' mean?
options: The lawn is mowed every Saturday
The lawn will mow every Saturday
The lawn was mowed last Saturday
Someone will mow the lawn on Saturday
questions.explanation: 'Wird' plus a participle (gemäht) is the present passive: the lawn has something done to it. The future would be 'wird ... mähen', with an infinitive.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'werden' used to form the passive?
questions.explanation: Only 'wird repariert' has a past participle, which makes the passive. 'Werden' with an infinitive forms the future, and on its own it means 'to become'.

questions.stem: 'Die Fenster wurden vom Hausmeister geputzt.' What does 'vom Hausmeister' tell you?
questions.explanation: In a passive sentence 'von' + dative names the person who carried out the action: the caretaker cleaned the windows. 'Wurden' marks the past.

questions.stem: 'Der Hund, den der Junge gestreichelt hat, gehört meiner Nachbarin.' Who did the stroking?
questions.explanation: 'Den' is accusative, so the dog is the object of 'gestreichelt'. 'Der Junge' is nominative and is the subject: the boy stroked the dog.

questions.stem: What does 'Das ist die Frau, deren Sohn in meiner Klasse ist' mean?
options: That is the woman whom my son knows from class
That is the woman whose class my son is in
That is the woman whose son is in my class
That is the woman who is in my son's class
questions.explanation: 'Deren' is the genitive relative pronoun for a feminine noun: 'whose'. It links 'Sohn' to the woman, and the son is the one in my class.

questions.stem: 'Wie heißt der Fluss, an dem Wien liegt?' What is being asked?
options: The name of the river Vienna lies on
Where the river near Vienna begins
Whether Vienna lies on a river
How far Vienna is from the river
questions.explanation: 'An dem Wien liegt' is a relative clause: 'on which Vienna lies'. The question asks for the river's name.

questions.stem: Compare 'Ich lasse den Hund im Garten spielen' and 'Ich lasse das Auto waschen'. What does 'lassen' mean in each?
options: Allow in the first; have something done in the second
Have something done in the first; allow in the second
questions.explanation: The dog plays because I let it, so 'lassen' means 'allow'. The car does not wash itself: I have someone wash it, so 'lassen' means 'have done'.

questions.stem: What does 'Ich hörte meine Schwester im Nebenzimmer telefonieren' mean?
options: I told my sister to make her call in the next room
I phoned my sister, who was in the next room
I heard my sister talking on the phone in the next room
I heard that my sister would phone from the next room
questions.explanation: A verb of perception such as 'hören' takes an object and a plain infinitive: I heard her phoning. There is no 'dass' clause and no command.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'In der Altstadt gibt es ___ schönen Markt.'?
questions.explanation: 'Es gibt' takes the accusative, and 'Markt' is masculine, so it is 'einen schönen Markt'. 'Ein' would be the nominative.

questions.stem: What does 'Es stimmt, dass das Wetter hier oft wechselt' mean?
options: It is true that the weather here often changes
It is a pity that the weather here often changes
It seems that the weather here often changes
It is possible that the weather here often changes
questions.explanation: 'Es stimmt, dass ...' means 'it is true that ...'. 'It is a pity' would be 'Es ist schade, dass ...'.

questions.stem: Why is it 'im Münchner Stadion' but 'im großen Stadion'?
options: Place names always take the strong dative ending
'Münchner' can only go with masculine nouns
Adjectives from place names end in -er and never change
'Münchner' is a noun in the genitive plural
questions.explanation: Adjectives made from town names add -er and keep that form in every case and gender: 'die Wiener Oper', 'im Kölner Dom'. Ordinary adjectives such as 'groß' take endings.

questions.stem: What does 'Das Betreten der Baustelle ist verboten' mean?
options: The building site entrance is closed
Walking past the building site is forbidden
Entering the building site is forbidden
Leaving the building site is forbidden
questions.explanation: 'Das Betreten' is the infinitive 'betreten' (to enter) used as a neuter noun, followed by a genitive: 'the entering of the building site'. Signs use this style often.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Beim ___ höre ich gern Musik.' ('while cooking')?
questions.explanation: 'Beim' + an infinitive used as a noun means 'while doing'. As a noun it takes a capital letter: 'beim Kochen'. 'Koch' is the cook, a person.

questions.stem: Which question asks what kind of car someone has?
questions.explanation: 'Was für ein' asks what kind of thing. 'Welches' asks which one out of a known group, and 'wessen' asks whose.

questions.stem: What does 'Ich habe weder Zeit noch Geld für den Urlaub' mean?
options: I have neither time nor money for the holiday
I have either time or money for the holiday
I have both time and money for the holiday
I have time but no money for the holiday
questions.explanation: 'Weder ... noch' means 'neither ... nor'. 'Entweder ... oder' is 'either ... or', and 'sowohl ... als auch' is 'both ... and'.

questions.stem: Which phrase means 'along the river'?
questions.explanation: 'Entlang' usually follows its noun and takes the accusative: 'den Fluss entlang'. 'Durch' is 'through', 'über' is 'over' or 'across', and 'um' is 'around'.
